title: Ezekiel 17:1–10
context: The LORD tells the prophet, addressed as son of man, to set a riddle and parable before the house of Israel. A great eagle crops the top of a cedar in Lebanon and carries it to a city of merchants, then plants a seed of the land that grows into a low, spreading vine. When a second great eagle appears, the vine bends its roots toward him for water. The LORD asks whether such a vine can prosper and answers that it will wither when the east wind touches it. The meaning is given by the text itself in 17:11-21. Both traditions read the parable as a lesson in covenant faithfulness and in the LORD’s rule over the affairs of kings.

verses.text: The LORD’s word came to me, saying,
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD’s word came to me, saying, Arminian readers note that the prophet does not invent the parable; the LORD gives both the riddle and, later, its interpretation.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that this formula opens a new unit. The prophet speaks in the first person, reporting the word as he received it, which places the authority of the riddle with the LORD.

verses.text: “Son of man, tell a riddle, and speak a parable to the house of Israel;
verses.arminianNotes: Son of man, tell a riddle, and speak a parable to the house of Israel; Arminian readers see the LORD using a story to engage the hearers’ minds, inviting them to ponder and respond.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that riddles both reveal and conceal, prompting the hearers to ask what they mean. The title son of man is the LORD’s usual way of addressing the prophet in this book.

verses.text: and say, ‘The Lord GOD says: “A great eagle with great wings and long feathers, full of feathers which had various colors, came to Lebanon and took the top of the cedar.
verses.arminianNotes: A great eagle with great wings and long feathers, Arminian readers see a powerful figure taking the top of the cedar, an image of a mighty ruler seizing what belongs to another land.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that 17:12 identifies the eagle as the king of Babylon. The cedar of Lebanon is commonly read as the royal house, though the text explains the image only in part.

verses.text: He cropped off the topmost of its young twigs, and carried it to a land of traffic. He planted it in a city of merchants.
verses.arminianNotes: He cropped off the topmost of its young twigs, and carried it to a land of traffic. Arminian readers see the removal of a young ruler from his land, planted in a city of merchants.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that 17:12 explains this as the king and princes taken to Babylon. Many readers connect the scene with the deportation of Jehoiachin described in 2 Kings 24:12-15.

verses.text: “ ‘ “He also took some of the seed of the land and planted it in fruitful soil. He placed it beside many waters. He set it as a willow tree.
verses.arminianNotes: He also took some of the seed of the land and planted it in fruitful soil. Arminian readers see the eagle establishing a new ruler from within the land, with conditions favorable for growth.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the image of a willow beside many waters. The seed is explained in 17:13 as one of the royal offspring, commonly identified with Zedekiah (2 Kings 24:17).

verses.text: It grew and became a spreading vine of low stature, whose branches turned toward him, and its roots were under him. So it became a vine, produced branches, and shot out sprigs.
verses.arminianNotes: It grew and became a spreading vine of low stature, Arminian readers see a kingdom allowed to flourish in a limited, dependent form, its branches turned toward the eagle that planted it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the low stature matches 17:14, where the kingdom is brought low so that it would stand by keeping the covenant. Modest security was offered within that arrangement.

verses.text: “ ‘ “There was also another great eagle with great wings and many feathers. Behold, this vine bent its roots toward him, and shot out its branches toward him, from the ground where it was planted, that he might water it.
verses.arminianNotes: Behold, this vine bent its roots toward him, Arminian readers see the vine’s choice to turn toward another great eagle for water, a decision that carried serious consequences.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that 17:15 links this to sending ambassadors into Egypt. The second eagle is commonly understood as the king of Egypt, though the text names Egypt and Pharaoh rather than a specific ruler.

verses.text: It was planted in a good soil by many waters, that it might produce branches and that it might bear fruit, that it might be a good vine.” ’
verses.arminianNotes: It was planted in a good soil by many waters, Arminian readers stress that the vine already had what it needed; its turning to the second eagle was not forced by want.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the repeated purpose phrases: that it might produce branches, bear fruit, and be a good vine. The vine’s restlessness appears all the more culpable against that provision.

verses.text: “Say, ‘The Lord GOD says: “Will it prosper? Won’t he pull up its roots and cut off its fruit, that it may wither, that all its fresh springing leaves may wither? It can’t be raised from its roots by a strong arm or many people.
verses.arminianNotes: Will it prosper? Arminian readers hear the LORD’s rhetorical question as a warning that disloyalty will bring ruin, its roots pulled up and its fruit cut off.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the statement that it can’t be raised from its roots by a strong arm or many people. No human help will be able to reverse the judgment once it falls.

verses.text: Yes, behold, being planted, will it prosper? Won’t it utterly wither when the east wind touches it? It will wither in the ground where it grew.” ’ ”
verses.arminianNotes: Yes, behold, being planted, will it prosper? Arminian readers see the east wind as an image of a destructive force that will wither the vine where it grew.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that the east wind is a common image for judgment in the prophets. The riddle ends in a question, leaving the hearers to reach its conclusion before the explanation.
